system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-10-28 01:41:00 to 2184-11-06 14:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of aggressive mesenteric fibromatosis, recurrent small bowel obstructions, and chronic TPN via a femoral catheter was admitted two days after a prior discharge due to a low-grade fever of 100.5°F noted at home. She had mild erythema at the femoral line site and ongoing nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs showed elevated creatinine (1.2) and leukocytosis (WBC 10.4), which improved with IV fluids and supportive care. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth. She remained afebrile throughout the hospitalization. The line site showed no signs of active infection, and pain during infusions was attributed to possible irritation or residual inflammation. She was discharged home after 48 hours of observation with stable vital signs, normalizing labs, and no infectious source identified. Outpatient follow-up was arranged for repeat line evaluation. Chronic conditions, including anemia, hypothyroidism, and migraines, remained stable.
problems: Other complications due to other vascular device, implant, and graft
Neoplasm of uncertain behavior of connective and other soft tissue
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with multiple small bowel obstructions in the
past presenting with abdominal pain.

COMPARISON:  Multiple priors, most recently ___.

FINDINGS:  The abdominal bowel gas pattern is nonspecific.  There is no
intraperitoneal free air.  Support catheters and stimulator devices are
unchanged.

IMPRESSION:  No obstruction or intraperitoneal free air.

GASTROSTOMY TUBE EXCHANGE

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ woman with chronic abdominal pain and
mesenteric sclerosis, presents for routine exchange of her gastrostomy tube
which is used for venting.  The patient concurrently complains of dull ache at
the insertion site of a triple-lumen tunneled right femoral venous line for
assessment.

Informed consent for the procedure was obtained after risks, benefits, and
potential complications had been discussed.  The patient was placed on the
angiographic table in supine position and skin of the anterior abdominal wall
around the gastrostomy tube insertion site was prepped and draped in a sterile
fashion.  Timeout protocol was carried out prior to the procedure according to
the ___ policy.

INTRAVENOUS MEDICATIONS ADMINISTERED DURING THE PROCEDURE:  None.

ANESTHESIA:  Topical, 2% lidocaine gel.

Existing 12 ___ gastrostomy tube was divided several
centimeters proximal to the skin entry and removed over a 0.035 ___
guidewire.  A new 12 ___ gastrostomy tube was advanced into
the stomach over the ___ guidewire.  Retention loop was formed and locked.
Insertion site was covered with sterile dressing.

The insertion area of the double-lumen right femoral tunneled venous line was
inspected and examined by palpation.  The patient complained of tenderness on
palpation, approximately 3 cm medial to the right femoral venous line
insertion site.  Fluoroscopic examination of the tunneled line demonstrated no
evidence of line fracture or migration.  There were no signs of skin infection
around the insertion site.

Dr. ___, the attending physician, supervised this interventional
procedure.

CONCLUSION:  Uncomplicated exchange of 12 ___ gastrostomy
tube over a guidewire.

EXCHANGE OF DOUBLE-LUMEN TUNNELED CENTRAL VENOUS CATHETER

INDICATION:  Indwelling right femoral tunneled central venous catheter with
exposed cuff.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr. ___ (attending
physician).  Dr. ___ was present during key moments of the procedure.

CONTRAST:  None.

SEDATION:  Moderate sedation with divided doses of intravenous ___ mcg
fentanyl and 2.5 mg Versed over 31 minutes, during which patient's hemodynamic
status was continuously monitored by a trained radiology nurse.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  Consent was obtained after explaining the benefits,
comparison, and alternatives.  Patient was placed supine on the imaging table
in the interventional suite.  Timeout was performed as per ___ protocol.

Initial scout fluoroscopic image demonstrated right femoral tunneled
hemodialysis catheter with its tip projecting over the expected location of
upper IVC.  Under aseptic conditions and after removing the indwelling
heparin, catheter was cut to introduce two 0.018 nitinol wires through the two
lumens.  Catheter remnant was removed over the wires to place a new 10 ___
double-lumen catheter.  Catheter tip was left in the upper IVC, and the cuff
about 3 cm from the exit site.  Catheter was secured by 0 silk sutures.  Site
was dressed in a sterile fashion.  Lumens were aspirated and flushed.  Patient
tolerated the procedure well.  No immediate post-procedure complication was
seen.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated exchange of indwelling 10 ___ double-lumen
tunneled right femoral central venous catheter with a similar but new one. 
Catheter may be used.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. You came in with worsening abdominal pain and vomiting—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain has been getting worse over the past week. It’s in my upper left and right belly, near my G tube. My usual morphine suppositories aren’t helping at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned vomiting every day for the last few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily for about a week now. Phenergan isn’t touching the nausea. I haven’t slept well because of the pain and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. We’ve reviewed your imaging—an X-ray showed some air-fluid levels, but no sign of a complete blockage. The surgical team doesn’t think you need surgery right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another bowel obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a complete one. It could be a partial slowdown, which fits with your history of sclerosing mesenteritis. We’ll manage your pain and nausea while keeping you on your TPN through your femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G tube output has also gone way up—1200 to 2200 cc a day. It used to be around 300.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s consistent with increased gut activity or irritation. We’ll keep monitoring it. For now, we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—so your gut can rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. But please, I need better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re starting IV Dilaudid every 4 hours and IV Phenergan every 6 hours. We’ll watch how you respond and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been so frustrated. This pain is constant and nothing’s working like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. It’s a lot to manage. We’ve asked social work to check in with you—they can help with emotional support and coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. Sometimes the emotional pain feels just as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain now after the first round of IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, maybe down to a 7 from a 10. But it’s still really uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the IV pain meds going and reassess. Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or kidney issues. We’ll continue TPN through your femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my line okay? I’ve had problems with it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it. There’s tenderness near the site, but no infection. However, the external part of the catheter looks worn. We may need to replace it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? It’s split before in the same spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re aware. It’s likely due to movement and positioning. We’ll plan for a replacement when you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re scheduled to replace your G tube. It was already due, and we think it’s a good time to do it while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’m worried about more pain afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a routine procedure. We’ll use local numbing gel. Most patients tolerate it well. We’ll give extra pain meds just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G tube was replaced successfully. The old one was removed and a new one placed over a guidewire. The site looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt some pressure, but not too bad. How’s the output now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still high, but we’ll keep monitoring. We’re starting to transition you back to rectal morphine and Phenergan since you’re tolerating things better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we increase the morphine? 20 mg isn’t cutting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing it to 25 mg every 6 hours as needed. We’ll watch for side effects like drowsiness or slow breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Pain is down, and you’re off IV meds. We’re keeping you on TPN and your new G tube is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’m still anxious about the femoral line. When will it be replaced?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling it for early next week. It’s important to fix it before it fails completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is now at a 3-4 with the 25 mg morphine. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finally something is helping. I’ve even slept a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep you on the current plan. Social work stopped by—they said you had a good talk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helped. I’m still overwhelmed, but I feel heard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge later this week. First, we’ll replace your femoral line tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Will it be done under sedation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get light sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed and won’t feel much. It’s a quick procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. And my other meds will stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. The only change is the morphine dose—now 25 mg PR every 6 hours as needed. Everything else continues as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You just had your femoral line replaced. It went smoothly—you tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t even remember much. Is it secure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, new catheter is in place, cuff positioned correctly. You can use it right away for TPN and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that the line is fixed and your pain is controlled, we’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your gastroenterologist and pain clinic as scheduled. And please follow up with your psychiatrist—we think that’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve realized how much the emotional side affects my pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Managing both is key. At home, keep using the 25 mg morphine PR as needed, but hold it if you’re drowsy or breathing slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my G tube and line care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—flush the G tube regularly, care for the skin, and do the ethanol lock for the line daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can manage that. Thank you for listening and adjusting my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We know this is a chronic struggle. We’re here to support you through each flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It means a lot. I’ll keep in touch with my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have all your prescriptions updated, especially the new morphine dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I don’t want to run out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’ll be filled before you leave. And if pain worsens, don’t hesitate to call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay in touch. I’ve learned to speak up when things aren’t working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Keep advocating for yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for respecting that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s how we get the best outcomes—together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel hopeful. That’s a good place to be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Rest up at home and take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for the support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your home health nurse is set up to help with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve already spoken to them. It’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We want you to feel supported at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge order processed. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with all my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, hopefully not in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so too. But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s comforting to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Always. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re rooting for you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of sclerosing mesenteritis, recurrent small bowel obstructions, and chronic TPN via a femoral catheter was admitted for worsening abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. Imaging showed no complete bowel obstruction, and the surgical team recommended medical management. She was initially NPO and treated with IV Dilaudid and Phenergan for pain and nausea. Her G tube was replaced as scheduled, and her morphine dose was increased to 25 mg PR every 6 hours due to inadequate pain control. A mechanical complication of her femoral central venous line—repeated splitting of the external portion—led to its replacement. She was transitioned back to home medications, including rectal morphine and Phenergan, with improved symptom control. Social work supported her emotional distress, which was multifactorial. She was discharged home with updated pain management, follow-up plans with gastroenterology, pain clinic, and mental health providers, and no pending studies.
